messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert, a 66-year-old European American software engineer, came to treatment after decades of carrying memories of a childhood marked by physical abuse from a caregiver, memories that had recently become harder to keep at bay. He described growing up in a home where discipline could turn sudden and cruel, where a raised hand, a sudden grab, or the feel of being cornered could mean pain. As an adult he had built a careful life with his wife, his work, and a reputation for being steady, yet he spoke of always sensing that danger could arrive without warning. That old lesson had become especially vivid in recent months when a brief flash of a childhood beating would come into his mind while he was at his desk, or when he noticed his own heart starting to pound in the middle of an otherwise ordinary day. At those moments, the body sensations themselves became alarming: the heat or chill of a room against his skin, the sudden racing in his chest, even a passing touch on the arm could pull him back into the same fear he knew as a boy. He said that when that happened, he could not trust his body not to betray him, and he would scan his surroundings for anything that might be used as a weapon, as if staying alert might keep him from being caught off guard again.

Over time Robert had come to believe that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next, and that belief shaped the way he moved through daily life. He had also come to think of himself as permanently an outsider now, someone set apart from the ease other people seemed to have, and he was increasingly convinced that people can’t be trusted. Those appraisals fed into a set of habits that narrowed his world. He avoided paying attention to or looking at his own body, because checking in with himself often led him straight to the sensations he feared. He steered away from seeing people he had socialised with before the event, even old acquaintances from work or neighbors from earlier years, because being around them stirred a sense that others were too close, too readable, too likely to judge or hurt. He also avoided any form of physical contact with others, including simple greetings that might put him in someone else’s reach. These habits brought short-term relief, but they also left him more alone and more certain that he did not belong among other people. The more he pulled back, the more outsider-like he felt, and the more his mistrust hardened into a rule for living.

That rule also sharpened his sense of danger. If he saw a kitchen knife on the counter, a tool in the garage, or even an unfamiliar object that could be used harmfully, his attention locked onto it. His body seemed to react before his mind had fully registered what he was seeing; his shoulders tightened and his heart started racing before he could think through whether there was any real threat. When someone at home or at work touched him unexpectedly, he reacted with alarm, sometimes jerking away before he could stop himself. Those startles reinforced his conviction that he had to stay on guard, and the fear of being caught unprepared brought back the same vivid, involuntary memories from childhood, with his caregiver’s anger and the felt sense of being trapped. He would then avoid his own body even more, trying not to notice the pounding in his chest or the tension in his limbs, but the harder he tried to shut his body out, the more unfamiliar and unsafe it felt. In his office, where he spent long hours at the computer, he found himself distracted by the temperature on his skin, by the urge to monitor the room for objects that could be dangerous, and by the wish to keep his distance from colleagues who might tap his shoulder or come up behind him.

By the time he sought help, Robert could see that his life had become organized around keeping danger at bay, yet the effort was exhausting and isolating. He felt ashamed that he had withdrawn from people he once knew, and troubled that even at work he was less at ease and less available than he used to be. What finally brought him in was the realization that his vigilance was never really letting him rest; the moment he noticed his heart racing, or caught an old memory rising up, or felt a hand on his arm, he was right back in the same world of threat. He was hoping for some way to feel safe in his own body again, and for help understanding why, even now, he still lived as though the danger from childhood could appear at any moment.
